title: Ames in Bellarmine Enervatus: will-seat with antecedent intellect assent — seeming clash
source_text: XI. In Bellarmino vero Enervato eadem de re sic philosophatur, Observandum est nos ita in voluntate fidem quae justificat collocare, ut antecedentem intellectus assensum ad fidem requiri doceamus, & vim ac virtutem fidei in intellectu consequentem agnoscamus. Qua utraque ratione fidem populariter ita describere solemus, quasi partim esset in intellectu, & partim in voluntate. Tom. 4. lib. 4. cap. 1. Ubi obiter notandum in priori loco, quem modo citavimus, Amesium ponere assensum, tanquam effectum fidei, in hoc vero posteriori, illum antecedentem intellectus assensum ad fidem requirere; inter quae videtur esse manifesta contradictio. Nam si assensus est effectum fidei, quomodo fidem antecedit? Nisi quis ista sic conciliare velit, ut dicat, juxta Amesium, assensum esse fidei effectum, quia sequitur unum ex illis quae fidem constituunt, ex Amesii mente, nempe piam illam erga Deum affectionem, quae facit, ut maxime valeat apud nos ipsius testimonium; Eundem tamen assensum, secundum Amesium, fidem antecedere, respectu aliorum actuum, quibus etiam constat fides qui sunt illa, quam vocat, Acquiescentia in Deo ad illud quod proponitur consequendum, & electio vel apprehensio rei ipsius, quae in testimonio nobis exhibetur.
pass_a_gloss: In Bellarmine Enervatus he philosophizes thus on the same matter: It is to be observed that we so place justifying faith in the will that we teach an antecedent intellect-assent is required for faith, and we acknowledge a consequent force and virtue of faith in the intellect. For both reasons we popularly describe faith as if partly in intellect and partly in will (tom. 4 book 4 ch. 1). Here note in passing that in the prior place just cited Ames treats assent as an effect of faith, but in this later place he requires antecedent intellect-assent for faith — between which there seems a manifest contradiction. For if assent is an effect of faith, how does it precede faith? Unless one would reconcile thus: according to Ames assent is faith's effect because it follows one of the things that constitute faith in his mind, namely that pious affection toward God which makes His testimony weigh most; yet the same assent, according to Ames, precedes faith with respect to the other acts that also constitute faith — namely what he calls resting in God for what is proposed to be obtained, and election or apprehension of the thing itself exhibited in the testimony.
pass_b_english: Ames (Bellarmine Enervatus 4.4.1) seats justifying faith in will yet requires antecedent intellect-assent and grants consequent intellect virtue.
Apparent clash with assent-as-effect is eased if assent follows pious affection but precedes resting/election acts.

choices.why: Seeming clash Ames softens by ordering affection→assent→rest/election.
